title: The Modernist Break
description: 1900–1940 — fragmenting form for a new age

concepts.title: What Modernism Was
concepts.contentHtml:
Literary Modernism is the loose movement, roughly 1900-1940, that rejected the techniques and assumptions of the 19th-century novel and poetry.

The Victorians had given readers a particular kind of confidence: a stable narrator, a knowable social world, plot moving toward resolution, a moral framework readers could share with the author. Modernism withdrew all of that.

What replaced it: fragmented form, multiple unreliable perspectives, mythic patterns interrupting daily life, fractured time, allusion to other works, deliberate difficulty. The reader was asked to do more interpretive work. The text refused to be transparent.

concepts.title: Historical Pressures
concepts.contentHtml:
The Modernists weren't just being difficult. They were responding to a world that had become unrecognizable.

The Great War (1914-1918) killed roughly 17 million people. Many of the brightest of a generation died in trenches for unclear gains. Postwar Europe had to absorb the failure of 19th-century progress narratives.

Freud's psychoanalysis (especially after The Interpretation of Dreams, 1900) suggested the conscious self was only the surface of a much darker unconscious.

Einstein's relativity (special, 1905; general, 1915) made the basic physical concepts of time and space context-dependent.

Industrial urbanization had reshaped daily life. Most people now lived in cities. The pace, anonymity, and scale of urban experience demanded new forms.

The Modernist response: the old forms can't represent the new reality. New forms are needed.

concepts.title: Make It New
concepts.contentHtml:
Ezra Pound's slogan — 'Make it new' — became the unofficial motto of the movement.

The phrase's meaning is layered. New forms, yes. But also: make older traditions new again, by reanimating them through fresh contact. Pound and Eliot were obsessive about the literary past. Their innovation came partly through reaching across centuries to revive Provençal troubadours, Latin poets, ancient Chinese verse.

This is one paradox of Modernism. It rejected the immediate Victorian past, but it embraced earlier traditions — pre-Romantic, classical, Eastern, primitive. Eliot's Waste Land draws on the Bible, Sanskrit, Wagner, Renaissance dramatists, French Symbolists. Joyce's Ulysses follows the structure of Homer's Odyssey.

The goal wasn't to abandon tradition but to expand and recombine it.

concepts.title: Difficulty as Method
concepts.contentHtml:
Modernism is famously hard. Eliot's Waste Land requires footnotes. Joyce's Ulysses assumes you've read Homer. Pound's Cantos jumps between five languages.

This was deliberate. The Modernists believed the modern world was difficult; literature that smoothed it into easy narrative would be a lie.

The difficulty also served other purposes:

– It demanded attentive readers, creating a serious literature against mass culture.

– It registered the genuine fragmentation of consciousness in industrial society.

– It opened space for ambiguity and multiple meanings the smoother prose closed off.

The cost: smaller audiences. Modernist works often had small first runs. Many bookshops wouldn't stock Ulysses at first. Public libraries refused it. Mass readership came later, often through educational institutions.

The trade-off has been debated since. Was Modernism's elitism necessary or self-defeating?

concepts.title: Centers and Edges
concepts.contentHtml:
Modernism wasn't a single movement but a network of overlapping movements, each centered in a particular place.

London: Pound, Eliot, the Imagists, Wyndham Lewis, Virginia Woolf, the Bloomsbury Group.

Paris: Proust, Gide, the Surrealists (Breton, Aragon), Joyce as exile, the Lost Generation Americans (Hemingway, Stein, Fitzgerald).

Vienna and Prague: Kafka, Musil, Rilke, Hofmannsthal.

Berlin: Brecht, Döblin, Benjamin (a critic central to thinking about Modernism).

Petersburg/Moscow: Akhmatova, Mandelstam, Mayakovsky, Babel.

New York: Stevens, Williams, the Harlem Renaissance (Hughes, Hurston).

The communications between centers were intense. Eliot, an American in London, finished The Waste Land in Lausanne. Joyce wrote in Trieste, Zurich, and Paris. The movement was international from the start.

title: Joyce & Stream of Consciousness
description: Ulysses, Dubliners, Portrait — the inward turn

concepts.title: Joyce's Career
concepts.contentHtml:
James Joyce (1882-1941) was born in Dublin and spent most of his adult life in voluntary exile — Trieste, Zurich, Paris. He wrote four major works in 25 years.

Dubliners (1914): 15 short stories about Dublin life. Naturalistic surface; technique already innovative.

A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916): the early life of Stephen Dedalus, told in prose that evolves with the protagonist.

Ulysses (1922): one day in Dublin, June 16, 1904. The central work of literary Modernism.

Finnegans Wake (1939): an experimental dream-language epic. The most extreme thing Joyce wrote, and probably the most argued-about.

Each book pushes farther than the last. Joyce's career is one of the most relentless artistic trajectories of the 20th century.

concepts.title: Dubliners and the Epiphany
concepts.contentHtml:
Dubliners contains stories of Dublin people at different stages of life — childhood, adolescence, mature life, death. Joyce called them studies in 'paralysis' — the city's stagnation registered in individual lives.

His technique: the stories build toward what Joyce called epiphanies — moments of sudden recognition, often crushing rather than illuminating. A boy realizes the woman he's been romanticizing isn't who he imagined. A lonely man reads of the death of a woman he once rejected and confronts what he has done with his life.

The most famous story, 'The Dead,' ends with Gabriel Conroy realizing his wife has carried for decades a love for a dead boy he can never match. Snow falls 'general all over Ireland.' The story's last paragraph is one of the most studied in modern fiction.

The epiphany became a recognizable literary technique. Many modern stories aim for this kind of sudden interior shift.

concepts.title: Ulysses
concepts.contentHtml:
Ulysses takes place on a single day — June 16, 1904 (now celebrated annually as 'Bloomsday' in Dublin). It follows Leopold Bloom, an advertising canvasser, through his ordinary errands and encounters; Stephen Dedalus, the young artist; and finally Bloom's wife Molly, in a closing chapter.

The structure parallels Homer's Odyssey. Bloom is Odysseus, Stephen is Telemachus, Molly is Penelope. Each chapter corresponds to a Homeric episode: the Cyclops becomes a narrow-sighted, bigoted Irish nationalist; the Sirens become barmaids in a hotel.

What makes the book work isn't the parallel — it's that the parallel illuminates how a perfectly ordinary day can be heroic. Bloom is small, henpecked, a Jew in a city that doesn't quite trust him. He's also kind, decent, and resourceful. By the day's end, the book has dignified his ordinariness without idealizing it.

Each chapter is in a different style. One is told in newspaper headlines. One is a hallucinatory drama set in a brothel. One imitates the entire history of English prose. The final chapter is Molly's 40-page interior monologue, almost unpunctuated.

concepts.title: Stream of Consciousness
concepts.contentHtml:
Joyce's most famous technique: stream of consciousness. Representing thought directly, in something close to its actual flow — fragmented, associative, simultaneous.

The technique wasn't entirely new. Edouard Dujardin (a French novelist) had used it in Les Lauriers sont coupés (1888); Henry James experimented with extreme interiority. But Joyce extended it dramatically.

What stream of consciousness can do: capture the texture of mind. Bloom watches a funeral and his thoughts skip from the body to the carriage horses to a memory of his dead son to thoughts of his current marriage to a phrase from a song.

What it can't do: communicate efficiently. The reader has to do constant interpretive work. References that occur in passing are sometimes unintroduced. Without footnotes or guides, large stretches of Ulysses are baffling.

Joyce knew this. He said he would 'keep the professors busy for centuries.' He has been right.

concepts.title: Finnegans Wake
concepts.contentHtml:
Joyce's last book, written over 17 years, is the most extreme thing he produced. Finnegans Wake (1939) abandons normal language in favor of a dream-tongue that mixes 60+ languages, puns at multiple levels, and almost no clear plot.

The opening sentence: 'riverrun, past Eve and Adam's, from swerve of shore to bend of bay, brings us by a commodius vicus of recirculation back to Howth Castle and Environs.'

The book's argument, more or less: history repeats. Specific characters (HCE, ALP, their twin sons) recur in different forms across periods. Dreams happen in language. The book is what a dreaming Dublin would say.

Many readers, including admirers of Ulysses, find Finnegans Wake impossible. The book's defenders say it rewards effort. The dispute has been continuous for nearly a century.

What's certain: it pushes Modernist ambition to its furthest reach. Whatever the form is at its limit, this is.

title: Eliot & Modernist Poetry
description: The Waste Land, Pound, the imagists

concepts.title: T.S. Eliot
concepts.contentHtml:
Thomas Stearns Eliot (1888-1965), an American who became British, was the central poet of literary Modernism in English.

His career divides into halves. The first — through the 1920s — produced the radical Modernist work: 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' (1915), The Waste Land (1922), 'The Hollow Men' (1925).

The second — after his 1927 conversion to Anglicanism — produced more religiously meditative work: Ash-Wednesday (1930), Four Quartets (1936-1942).

He also wrote criticism, essays, and verse drama. He won the Nobel Prize in 1948. His position in 20th-century letters was uniquely authoritative — for several decades, Eliot's taste largely set what counted as serious poetry.

concepts.title: Prufrock
concepts.contentHtml:
'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' (written 1910-11, published 1915) is often called the first Modernist poem in English.

The speaker is a middle-aged man in an indeterminate social setting, perhaps about to make a romantic overture, perhaps unable to. His monologue moves through self-doubt, self-mockery, paralysis, fantasy.

The poem's openings: 'Let us go then, you and I, / When the evening is spread out against the sky / Like a patient etherized upon a table.' The simile is shocking — not 19th-century romantic at all. The mood is internal, modern, urban, neurotic.

'I have measured out my life with coffee spoons.' 'Do I dare to eat a peach?' The lines are quotable because they have the precision Modernist verse aspired to.

The poem ends with mermaids singing 'each to each' — and Prufrock noting they will not sing to him. Ineffective masculinity, the lyric impulse failing on contact with modern life.

concepts.title: The Waste Land
concepts.contentHtml:
The Waste Land (1922) is the central Modernist poem in English — and probably the most analyzed poem of the 20th century.

It's 434 lines in five sections. Voices interrupt voices. Multiple languages appear. Allusions span from the Bible through Wagner through Sanskrit. There is no single narrator. There is no sustained narrative.

What it depicts: a postwar London (and post-everything spiritual landscape) in fragments. Sterile sex, dead men, prophecies that don't come, rituals that have lost meaning. A culture in collapse.

Pound edited the poem heavily — cut perhaps half of an earlier draft. Eliot dedicated the published version 'For Ezra Pound, il miglior fabbro' ('the better craftsman'). Without Pound's edits, the poem might be much less than it became.

The poem's conclusion — 'Shantih shantih shantih' (a Sanskrit blessing meaning 'the peace that passeth understanding') — has been read as resignation, as authentic spiritual moment, as ironic gesture. The poem refuses to settle the question.

concepts.title: Pound and the Imagists
concepts.contentHtml:
Ezra Pound (1885-1972) was the catalyst of literary Modernism. Less of a great poet than Eliot in many readers' view, but indispensable as organizer, editor, theorist, and provocateur.

His early manifesto was Imagism. The principles, in his summary:

1. Direct treatment of the 'thing.' No abstraction without an image to anchor it.

2. Use absolutely no word that does not contribute to the presentation.

3. As regards rhythm: to compose in the sequence of the musical phrase, not in the sequence of a metronome.

This was a manifesto against Victorian wordiness and abstraction. The imagist poems are short, sharp, focused.

Pound's longer career was the Cantos — a 120-section poem written over 50 years, mixing Chinese history, troubadour poetry, fascist economics (he was sympathetic to Mussolini), and personal lament. It's one of the great 20th-century failures-and-achievements simultaneously: brilliant in places, incoherent in others, and shadowed by his political crimes.

concepts.title: Other Modernist Poets
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond Eliot and Pound:

William Carlos Williams: 'No ideas but in things.' Williams rejected what he saw as Eliot's European cosmopolitanism in favor of an American idiom of plain speech. 'so much depends / upon // a red wheel / barrow.'

Wallace Stevens: a Hartford insurance executive who wrote some of the most philosophical poetry in English. Harmonium (1923), 'Sunday Morning,' 'The Idea of Order at Key West.' The making of poetic order from chaos was his constant subject.

Marianne Moore: dense, formal, idiosyncratic. 'I, too, dislike it,' her poem 'Poetry' famously begins. A virtuoso of syllabic verse.

Hart Crane: ambitious, ecstatic, doomed. The Bridge (1930) attempted to write an American epic on the spiritual significance of the Brooklyn Bridge. He drowned at sea at 32.

H.D. (Hilda Doolittle): imagism's purest practitioner; later wrote longer hermetic poems integrating mythology and psychoanalysis.

The Modernist poetry scene was much wider than Eliot. Each of these poets opened directions later poets followed.

title: Woolf & Interiority
description: Mrs Dalloway, To the Lighthouse, the moments of being

concepts.title: Virginia Woolf
concepts.contentHtml:
Virginia Woolf (1882-1941) was the central woman novelist of British Modernism. Her major novels — Mrs Dalloway (1925), To the Lighthouse (1927), The Waves (1931), Orlando (1928), Between the Acts (1941) — explore consciousness in ways the Victorian novel hadn't.

She also wrote essential criticism. A Room of One's Own (1929) argued that 'a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction' — one of the founding texts of feminist literary thought. Three Guineas (1938) extended the argument toward war and patriarchy.

She was at the center of the Bloomsbury Group, an interconnected circle of writers, artists, and economists — Lytton Strachey, Roger Fry, John Maynard Keynes, E.M. Forster — that produced an enormous amount of British intellectual culture.

concepts.title: Mrs Dalloway
concepts.contentHtml:
Mrs Dalloway takes place over a single June day in 1923 London. Clarissa Dalloway, an upper-class woman in her fifties, prepares for a party that evening. Septimus Smith, a shell-shocked WWI veteran, walks the same city.

They never meet. Clarissa hears of his suicide at her party. The novel ends with her, somehow recognizing her connection to him, returning to her guests.

The technique: free indirect discourse drifts continuously between consciousnesses. We're inside Clarissa, then her old love Peter Walsh, then Septimus, then his wife Rezia, then various passersby, often within a single page. The narrative voice belongs to no one and everyone.

What the novel does: makes a single ordinary day reverberate with depth. Clarissa's party isn't trivial in the world Woolf builds. Memory invades present action. Past loves and dead friends and unspoken regrets are all simultaneous with the moment.

It's the Modernist novel that most makes interiority feel like the basic stratum of existence.

concepts.title: To the Lighthouse
concepts.contentHtml:
To the Lighthouse (1927) is many readers' favorite Woolf novel. It has three parts.

Part 1, 'The Window': a single afternoon and evening at the Ramsay family's summer house in the Hebrides. Mrs Ramsay (a portrait of Woolf's mother) holds the family together; her son James wants to go to the lighthouse the next day; the philosopher Mr Ramsay says they can't because of the weather. James never forgives him.

Part 2, 'Time Passes': ten years compressed into a few pages. World War I happens. Mrs Ramsay dies. Two of her children die. The house decays. All this is conveyed in spare prose, with parenthetical brackets containing the deaths.

Part 3, 'The Lighthouse': the surviving family returns. James and his sister Cam finally make the trip to the lighthouse with their father. The painter Lily Briscoe finishes a painting she started ten years earlier. The novel ends.

The book is about loss, time, and the small human attempts to fix experience against the dissolving force of years. The middle section is one of the most extraordinary passages in 20th-century fiction.

concepts.title: Moments of Being
concepts.contentHtml:
Woolf had a phrase for her central artistic concern: moments of being.

Most life, she argued, is 'non-being' — automatic, unattended, lost to memory. But occasionally, a moment of being arrives. The world becomes vivid. Things are seen with extraordinary clarity. The self feels simultaneously dissolved and intensified.

Her novels are organized around such moments. Mrs Ramsay holds her family during a dinner; the boeuf en daube is perfect; for that moment everything is right. Lily Briscoe finally sees how to finish her painting. Clarissa hears the news of Septimus's death.

The technique requires extreme attention to perception. Woolf's prose, at its best, makes the reader feel that they are seeing something for the first time. This isn't description; it's an attempt to make perception itself the subject.

The Modernist project of representing consciousness, in Woolf, becomes a project of slowing experience down to where its texture can be felt.

concepts.title: Woolf's Reception
concepts.contentHtml:
Woolf's reputation has shifted across decades.

In her lifetime: respected as one of the major Modernists, but with reservations — some critics found her precious or limited.

Mid-20th century: her star declined somewhat against Joyce and Eliot. She was sometimes treated as a less rigorous secondary modernist.

From the 1970s onward: feminist criticism repositioned her as a major figure. A Room of One's Own became a foundational feminist text. The novels were reread for their representation of gender and consciousness.

21st century: Woolf is now generally considered alongside Joyce as the two pinnacles of British Modernist fiction — sometimes ahead of him, depending on the reader. Mrs Dalloway in particular has become one of the most-taught modern novels.

The arc — from contemporary regard to dimming to renewed centrality — is common in literary reception. Reading a writer's work freshly often requires waiting out the period when fashion has temporarily dismissed them.

title: Kafka & European Modernism
description: Trial and Metamorphosis — bureaucracy and the unreal

concepts.title: Kafka
concepts.contentHtml:
Franz Kafka (1883-1924) wrote in German in Prague. He worked at an insurance institute, wrote at night, and asked his friend Max Brod to burn his manuscripts when he died. Brod ignored the request.

The major works:

The Metamorphosis (1915): a novella in which a traveling salesman, Gregor Samsa, wakes up as an enormous insect.

The Trial (published 1925, posthumously): Joseph K. is arrested by an inscrutable authority for an unnamed crime. The trial drags on. He is eventually executed.

The Castle (1926, posthumous): a land surveyor named K. arrives at a village and tries to reach a castle that supposedly hired him. He never gets there.

Plus stories — 'In the Penal Colony,' 'A Hunger Artist,' 'A Country Doctor,' 'Before the Law,' 'The Burrow.' Each unforgettable, each unsettling.

concepts.title: The Kafkaesque
concepts.contentHtml:
The adjective 'Kafkaesque' has entered general English. It describes a particular mode of nightmare: bureaucratic, absurd, inescapable, with an outwardly normal surface.

The features:

– A protagonist who is small, anxious, ordinary.

– An authority that is opaque, impersonal, possibly arbitrary.

– Rules that exist but can't be fully understood.

– A setting that is realistic in detail but dreamlike in logic.

– Increasing entrapment despite the protagonist's efforts.

What makes Kafka different from other surreal writers: he tells these stories in calm, even tones. There is no expressionist screaming. The bureaucracy of The Trial sounds like a real bureaucracy. The horror is the reasonableness with which the unreasonable is described.

The Kafkaesque has turned out to describe much of 20th-century experience. Totalitarian states, complex modern bureaucracies, opaque corporate structures, automated denial of services — all feel Kafkaesque. He saw something coming.

concepts.title: The Metamorphosis
concepts.contentHtml:
The opening of The Metamorphosis: 'When Gregor Samsa woke one morning from troubled dreams, he found himself transformed in his bed into a monstrous vermin.'

The story doesn't explain. Gregor is not surprised in any natural way. His main concern, in the first pages, is being late for work.

What follows isn't horror — Gregor is the horror, not the witness — but family logistics. His sister feeds him. His parents grow increasingly impatient. He hides under the sofa to spare them. They reduce his food. Eventually they wish he were dead. He dies. They go for a country walk and feel relieved.

Kafka's mode is to take a fantastic premise and follow its emotional and social consequences with realist precision. The transformation isn't a metaphor for one thing; it's an experience the reader has to live with on the story's own terms.

Generations of readers have applied the story to their own situations — alienation from work, family burden, depression, illness. The story accommodates all of these.

concepts.title: Other European Modernists
concepts.contentHtml:
European Modernism extended well beyond Kafka.

Marcel Proust (France, 1871-1922): In Search of Lost Time — seven volumes, 4,000 pages. The narrator's involuntary memory traces French aristocratic society from the 1870s to WWI. The opening madeleine scene is the most famous moment of literary memory in the 20th century.

Robert Musil (Austria, 1880-1942): The Man Without Qualities. A massive unfinished novel about pre-WWI Vienna. Encyclopedic, ironic, philosophical.

Hermann Broch (Austria, 1886-1951): The Death of Virgil. The Roman poet's last hours, written in dense, unparagraphed prose.

Italo Svevo (Italy, 1861-1928): Zeno's Conscience. An Italian businessman's attempts at self-analysis through the new medium of psychoanalysis. Joyce championed Svevo and helped him reach a wider audience.

Knut Hamsun (Norway, 1859-1952): Hunger, Mysteries. Anticipates much of European Modernism by decades. Later disgraced by his fascist sympathies.

European Modernism produced more masterpieces than any single canon can comfortably hold.

concepts.title: Why It Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
European Modernism gave us forms that contemporary literature still draws on:

The unreliable narrator: a narrator we can't fully trust. Conrad's Marlow, Nabokov's Humbert, Ishiguro's Stevens.

Time-shifting: complex non-chronological structures. Faulkner, contemporary memoirists, film.

Bureaucratic surrealism: Kafka's mode survives in figures from Vonnegut to Saunders to Borges.

Long fictional autobiography: Proust shaped a tradition that runs through Knausgaard.

The fragmented modernist novel: still a default option.

Most contemporary serious fiction is Modernism softened. The narrator may be more stable, the prose more readable, the surface less obviously experimental. But the techniques — interior consciousness, free indirect discourse, time manipulation, refusal of moral certainty — descend from this period.

Reading the great Modernists isn't a duty toward the past. It's coming back to the source of how the modern novel works.

concepts.title: American Modernism
concepts.contentHtml:
American Modernism partly overlapped with European but had its own character. The trauma of WWI affected America less directly. American writers had to ask different questions about modernity.

The major novelists came of age in the 1920s. Many spent time in Paris during what Gertrude Stein called the 'Lost Generation.' They returned with European techniques and applied them to American material — small towns, Southern decay, jazz-age New York, post-frontier disillusionment.

What unifies them: a sense that the optimistic 19th-century American story — work hard, prosper, marry, build the nation — had broken. Their books register the collapse, often with painful clarity.

concepts.title: Hemingway
concepts.contentHtml:
Ernest Hemingway (1899-1961) developed perhaps the most influential prose style of the 20th century.

His method: short sentences, concrete nouns, few adjectives, no overt psychology. The 'iceberg' theory — show one-eighth above water, leave seven-eighths below. The reader infers what's not stated.

Major works: The Sun Also Rises (1926), A Farewell to Arms (1929), For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940), The Old Man and the Sea (1952). Plus the short stories — 'Hills Like White Elephants,' 'A Clean, Well-Lighted Place,' the Nick Adams stories.

His best work depicts characters wounded by war, by love, by failure, who continue to act with grace within their limits. Code heroes who endure without complaint. The style enacts the stoicism the characters require.

Influence: enormous. Cormac McCarthy, Joan Didion, Raymond Carver, much of mid-20th-century American minimalism descend from him. Generations of fiction-writing students have been told to 'leave out anything you don't need,' which is Hemingway's lesson.

Reaction has set in periodically. He's been accused of macho posturing, sentimentality beneath the toughness, formulaic repetition. The criticism has merit. The power of the best work survives it.

concepts.title: Fitzgerald
concepts.contentHtml:
F. Scott Fitzgerald (1896-1940) was the chronicler of the Jazz Age and its aftermath. His four completed novels — This Side of Paradise, The Beautiful and Damned, The Great Gatsby, Tender Is the Night — and his short stories trace the giddy 1920s into the depressed 1930s.

The Great Gatsby (1925) is his masterpiece and one of the most-taught American novels. A bond trader, Nick Carraway, observes his neighbor Jay Gatsby — a self-invented millionaire trying to win back the woman he loved years before. Gatsby's elaborate parties, his dream, his death are filtered through Nick's increasingly disillusioned perspective.

The novel works on multiple levels: a love story, a critique of the American Dream, a meditation on class, a study of self-invention. The final line — 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past' — is among the most quoted in American literature.

Fitzgerald's late life was difficult. Heavy drinking, his wife Zelda's mental illness, declining sales. He died of a heart attack at 44. His reputation, weak at the end of his life, recovered after his death.

concepts.title: Faulkner
concepts.contentHtml:
William Faulkner (1897-1962) wrote about Yoknapatawpha County, Mississippi — a fictional version of his actual home in Oxford. Across about a dozen novels and many stories, he constructed a complete imaginative world: families, histories, slave-and-master pasts, decay, race, and persistent guilt.

The major novels: The Sound and the Fury (1929), As I Lay Dying (1930), Light in August (1932), Absalom, Absalom! (1936). All technically demanding.

The Sound and the Fury opens with 60+ pages of the consciousness of Benjy Compson, a mentally disabled man who can't track time. Sentences shift between decades without warning. The reader has to assemble the family history from scattered impressions.

Absalom, Absalom! tells the story of Thomas Sutpen, a self-made plantation owner, through multiple narrators who never quite agree. The novel becomes an inquiry into how stories about the past get made.

Faulkner won the Nobel Prize in 1949. His 1950 acceptance speech argued that literature must concern itself with 'the human heart in conflict with itself' — that this alone is worth writing about. Despite his difficulty and pessimism, the speech offered a kind of credo.

concepts.title: Other Voices
concepts.contentHtml:
The Lost Generation was not just three white men.

Gertrude Stein (1874-1946): the avant-garde center. Her Paris salon hosted everyone. Her own writing — Tender Buttons, The Making of Americans — was extreme even among Modernists.

Ezra Pound, T.S. Eliot: also American expatriates of this period, on the poetry side.

The Harlem Renaissance (1918-1937): the great flowering of African American literature. Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Claude McKay, Countee Cullen, Jean Toomer's Cane. Modernist techniques applied to Black American experience.

Willa Cather: not always grouped with the Modernists, but a major novelist of the period — My Ántonia, Death Comes for the Archbishop.

John Dos Passos: the U.S.A. trilogy — collage, newsreels, multiple plotlines. American Modernism's most ambitious experiment with form.

John Steinbeck: more conventional in form, but a major chronicler of the Depression — The Grapes of Wrath, Of Mice and Men.

The American canon of the 1920s-1940s was richer and more diverse than the standard 'Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Faulkner' summary suggests.
